forces: Orchestra with E♭ clarinet, bells and expanded percussion
intro: Berlioz brings his artist to his own funeral, surrounded by witches, monsters and the beloved, now laughing in an E♭ clarinet. Deep bells announce the Dies irae; the funeral chant ends up dancing with the witches.

cues.title: Trembling strings at a funeral
cues.text: Muted violins and violas tremble high above the cellos and basses, whose quick figures climb out of the depths. Soft timpani strokes interrupt them. Berlioz’s artist dreams that witches and monsters have gathered for his funeral.
cues.evidence: Movement V, bars 1–20, Michel Austin’s score transcription: http://www.hberlioz.com/scosupp/symfantas5.pdf . Funeral gathering: Berlioz’s programme, part V, http://www.hberlioz.com/Scores/fantasf.htm
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The beloved joins the witches
cues.text: The idée fixe returns in the clarinets, covered in trills and grace notes. After the first glimpse on C clarinet, the small E♭ clarinet turns it into a quick, grotesque dance. Berlioz’s beloved has joined the sabbath.
cues.evidence: Movement V, bars 21–78, including the first C-clarinet glimpse and the later E♭-clarinet statement; Michel Austin’s score transcription and Berlioz’s programme.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A symphony of Faust
cues.text: In February 1829 Berlioz tells his friend Humbert Ferrand that “a descriptive symphony of Faust” is fermenting in his head, and that he means it to strike the musical world with terror. The symphony keeps Goethe’s Faust for its last movement, which echoes the Walpurgis Night scene.
cues.evidence: Berlioz to Humbert Ferrand, 2 February 1829 (Correspondance générale no. 113), in Michel Austin’s translation; Austin on the Faustian last movement and Goethe’s Walpurgis Night: http://www.hberlioz.com/Scores/sfantastique.htm . Berlioz, Mémoires, chapter 26: https://fr.wikisource.org/wiki/M%C3%A9moires_de_Hector_Berlioz/26

cues.title: Bells behind the stage
cues.text: Bassoons, cellos and basses sink to a long, quiet note. Deep bells enter behind the stage, sounding C and G. Their tolling leaves room for scraps of the coming dance in the strings.
cues.evidence: Movement V, bars 87–126, especially the offstage bell part from bar 102 and intervening string fragments; Michel Austin’s score transcription, pp. 19–22.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The funeral chant arrives
cues.text: Four bassoons and two ophicleides intone the Dies irae, the chant from the Mass for the Dead. Its long notes move together above the bells. Later statements shorten those notes and hand the tune to brighter wind and brass voices.
cues.evidence: Movement V, bars 127–221, headed Dies irae, begins with four bassoons and two ophicleides; later statements diminish the note values. Modern performances use tubas for the ophicleide parts. http://www.hberlioz.com/scosupp/symfantas5.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The witches dance in fugue
cues.text: Cellos and double basses start the witches’ round. Violas follow, then violins: each entry begins while the earlier players continue. A tune built from quick rising notes and a turn becomes a dance crowded with pursuing voices.
cues.evidence: Movement V, Ronde du Sabbat from bar 241; successive string entries in Michel Austin’s score transcription, pp. 34–38.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Berlioz changes the printed story
cues.text: In 1845 Berlioz insists that the audience receive his programme before hearing the symphony. In 1855 he allows the symphony to stand alone, without the explanation. The story changes too: in the later version, the whole work takes place in an opium dream.
cues.evidence: Berlioz’s 1845 and 1855 programme prefaces, and their differing placement of the opium dream: http://www.hberlioz.com/Scores/fantasf.htm

cues.title: Liszt applauds
cues.text: The day before the première, nineteen-year-old Franz Liszt called on Berlioz; they had never met. Berlioz spoke of Goethe’s Faust. Liszt admitted he had not read it, and soon loved it as much as Berlioz did. At the concert his applause made the whole hall notice him.
cues.evidence: Berlioz, Mémoires, chapter 31 (Liszt’s visit on the eve of the concert, his applause, and the Bal, Marche au supplice and Sabbat making “une grande sensation”): https://fr.wikisource.org/wiki/M%C3%A9moires_de_Hector_Berlioz/31 . Liszt was born on 22 October 1811: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franz_Liszt

cues.title: Funeral chant against witches’ dance
cues.text: The wind and brass hold the Dies irae in broad notes while the strings race through the witches’ round beneath it. Berlioz writes both names above the score. The solemn chant and the quick dance now occupy the same bars.
cues.evidence: Movement V, combined Dies irae and Ronde du Sabbat from bar 414, Michel Austin’s score transcription, pp. 59–64. The heading explicitly names both tunes.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The wood of the bow
cues.text: For one late episode, the violins and violas strike their strings with the wood of their bows: col legno. The high repeated notes become a dry rattle. Woodwinds trill above plucked cello and bass notes.
cues.evidence: Movement V, bars 444–460, col legno in violins and violas; wind trills and pizzicato low strings in bars 448–459. Michel Austin’s score transcription, pp. 64–66, and commentary at http://www.hberlioz.com/Scores/sfantastique.htm
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The bows bite again
cues.text: The woodwinds have a brief turn alone, then the strings resume bowing, fortissimo. Brass chords and timpani join them. The last pages drive towards C major, with the whole orchestra hammering out the close.
cues.evidence: Movement V, final passage from bar 460: woodwind episode, arco fortissimo from bar 467 and C-major ending; Michel Austin’s score transcription, pp. 66–76.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: The clarinet begins a grotesque recollection
transitions.from: Intro · Muted tremolos and strange calls
transitions.how: The slow, chromatic introduction yields to a clarinet glimpse of the idée fixe over quiet drums. An orchestral outburst interrupts it. The E♭ clarinet then takes the tune in a quick dance, with oboe chords and running bassoon figures; the score has moved into E♭ major.
transitions.evidence: Movement V, bars 21–54; Michel Austin’s score transcription, pp. 7–12, including the change to three flats and E♭-clarinet statement.

transitions.title: The low instruments prepare the bells
transitions.to: Link · Deep bells toll C and G
transitions.how: The brilliant E♭-major episode breaks off. Bassoons, cellos and double basses descend in long notes, fading to pianississimo. Bells marked “behind the stage” begin tolling C and G; short string figures stir between their strokes.
transitions.evidence: Movement V, bars 79–126, especially the low descending line at bars 87–101 and bells from bar 102; Michel Austin’s score transcription.

transitions.title: Bassoons answer the funeral bells
transitions.from: Link · Deep bells toll C and G
transitions.to: B · Bassoons intone the Dies irae
transitions.how: The C and G bells leave space for four bassoons and two ophicleides to begin the Dies irae. They play the chant together in long notes, marked forte. High strings and woodwinds remain silent for this first statement.
transitions.evidence: Movement V, bars 123–147, Michel Austin’s score transcription, p. 22.

transitions.title: The basses start the round
transitions.from: B · Bassoons intone the Dies irae
transitions.to: C · The witches begin their round
transitions.how: An orchestral chord gives way to the Ronde du Sabbat in C major. Cellos and basses begin its quick rising figure, with a sharply accented turn at the top. Violas enter next, then violins, while the earlier parts keep dancing.
transitions.evidence: Movement V, bars 240–262, Michel Austin’s score transcription, pp. 34–38: new key signature and successive string entries.

transitions.title: Quiet horns recall the chant
transitions.from: C · The witches begin their round
transitions.to: B + C · Horns summon chant and dance
transitions.how: The round subsides into held string and bassoon notes. Solo horns recall the chant in short phrases; divided violas begin to move beneath them. Cellos and a quiet bass-drum roll join the gathering figures, preparing the return of the dance and chant together.
transitions.evidence: Movement V, bars 347–379, Michel Austin’s score transcription, pp. 52–53: horn phrases, divided violas, solo cellos and bass drum.

transitions.title: The strings return to their bows
transitions.from: B + C · Horns summon chant and dance
transitions.to: Coda · Bows, brass and the final rush
transitions.how: After the col legno rattle, the strings pause for a quick woodwind phrase. They return arco, fortissimo, against brass chords and timpani. Cellos and basses bow the low notes again; the closing rush leads to the final C-major chords.
transitions.evidence: Movement V, bars 460–524, especially arco at bar 467; Michel Austin’s score transcription, pp. 66–76.

source.title: Berlioz, Songe d’une nuit du Sabbat — orchestral score
source.locator: Introduction, bars 1–20; idée fixe, bars 21–78; bells from bar 102; Dies irae from bar 127; witches’ round from bar 241; combined themes from bar 414; col legno, bars 444–460. The tuba symbol shows the two ophicleide parts; percussion includes the bells.

timeline.note: Muted upper strings tremble above rising cello and bass figures and soft timpani strokes.
A C clarinet recalls the idée fixe over quiet drums; the strings join the crescendo.
The E♭ clarinet turns the beloved’s melody into a dance, with trills and grace notes.
Bassoons, cellos and basses descend and fade; deep bells toll C and G.
Four bassoons and two ophicleides intone the Dies irae above the bells.
The chant passes through brass and woodwinds in successively shorter notes.
Cellos and basses begin the round; violas and violins enter in turn.
Woodwinds, brass and percussion join the strings’ imitative dance.
Horn calls sound over held bassoon and string notes; violas, cellos and bass drum begin the build-up.
Wind and brass carry the funeral chant while strings play the witches’ round.
Violins and violas strike with the wood of their bows; woodwinds trill above plucked bass notes.
The strings resume bowing; wind, brass and percussion join the final C-major rush.

quote.text: Shakespeare struck me like a thunderbolt.
quote.source: Berlioz, Mémoires, chapter XVIII, recalling the Paris performances of September 1827; our translation

composer.background:
When the young Hector Berlioz read aloud the death of Dido, his voice failed him. His father closed the book and announced that he was tired, allowing the boy to escape without having to explain his tears. Berlioz remembered the kindness in his Mémoires. Louis Berlioz was a doctor in La Côte-Saint-André, between Lyon and Grenoble, and taught his son Latin, history and geography. He expected Hector to follow him into medicine. The boy learnt flute and guitar, pored over maps of distant islands and took Virgil’s abandoned queen personally.

In 1821 he went to Paris to study medicine. His first visit to the dissecting room at the Pitié hospital, he later wrote, ended with a flight through a window. On the second visit he managed perfectly well. Music was the more durable obstacle. He heard Salieri’s Les Danaïdes at the Opéra and began singing its airs over the cadavers. At the Conservatoire library he copied and memorised Gluck’s scores. His father argued, threatened and withheld support. Hector took composition lessons with Jean-François Le Sueur.
